overview: Two very different weapons bacteria use to cause disease — one is actively secreted, the other is a structural component released on cell death.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Proteins actively secreted by living bacteria (both Gram-positive and Gram-negative) that damage host cells or disrupt normal function.
aspects.valueB: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) components of the Gram-negative outer membrane, released mainly when the bacterial cell lyses or dies.

aspects.label: Chemical Composition
aspects.valueB: Lipopolysaccharide (specifically the lipid A portion is the toxic component).

aspects.label: Source
aspects.valueA: Secreted by living Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria.
aspects.valueB: Structural part of the Gram-negative outer membrane; released upon cell lysis or death.

aspects.label: Mechanism
aspects.valueA: Highly specific mechanisms — e.g. enzymatic disruption, blocking protein synthesis, or interfering with neurotransmission, depending on the specific toxin.
aspects.valueB: General, non-specific immune activation — triggers cytokine release (e.g. via binding to host TLR4), which can lead to fever, inflammation, and in severe cases septic shock.

aspects.label: Potency
aspects.valueA: Often highly potent even in extremely small amounts, due to specific molecular targets.
aspects.valueB: Generally less potent per molecule than exotoxins, but effects scale with the amount of Gram-negative bacterial lysis.

aspects.label: Heat Stability
aspects.valueA: Generally heat-labile — many are denatured/inactivated by heat.
aspects.valueB: Generally heat-stable — LPS withstands heat that would denature most proteins.

aspects.label: Toxoid/Vaccine Potential
aspects.valueA: Can often be inactivated (toxoided) while retaining immunogenicity, forming the basis of some vaccines.
aspects.valueB: Not typically toxoided into a vaccine antigen in the same way, given its non-protein, general-immune-activating nature.

aspects.label: Clinical Significance
aspects.valueA: Responsible for many specific disease presentations (e.g. specific paralysis, specific tissue damage) tied to the individual toxin's target.
aspects.valueB: Associated with fever and systemic inflammatory responses; large-scale release is linked to septic shock in Gram-negative infections.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Actively secreted protein with a highly specific mechanism.
aspects.valueB: Structural lipopolysaccharide released on cell death, causing general immune activation.

aspects.label: Primary Purpose / Indication
aspects.valueA: Explains organism-specific disease presentations tied to a distinct toxin.
aspects.valueB: Explains general systemic inflammatory/febrile responses in Gram-negative infections.

aspects.label: Limitations / Pitfalls
aspects.valueA: Presence of a gene encoding a toxin does not guarantee clinically significant expression in every strain/context.
aspects.valueB: Endotoxin activity correlates with bacterial load and lysis, not with a single discrete 'dose' the way a secreted toxin might be measured.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Exotoxin = protein, specific, often heat-labile, can be toxoided. Endotoxin = LPS, general, heat-stable, tied to Gram-negative cell death.
overlay.memoryTrick: "Exo exits the cell on purpose. Endo only comes out when the cell dies."
overlay.commonMisconception: Endotoxin is not 'released' the way exotoxins are secreted — it's a structural piece of the cell that becomes a problem specifically when the cell breaks apart.
